title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: Autopilot agent and Office in Copilot ship as Microsoft rebuilds the Copilot app around autonomous work
subtitle: At last week's conference Microsoft moved Home and Office in Copilot to general availability and began rolling out Autopilot, an always-on agent with its own Entra identity, through its Frontier program.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On November 17 at Ignite 2026 in San Francisco, Microsoft moved Home and Office in Copilot to general availability — folding Word, Excel and PowerPoint into the Copilot app — and began shipping Autopilot, a fully autonomous, always-on agent with its own Microsoft Entra identity, memory, and tool ecosystem, through the Frontier early-access program. Agent 365 Business Analytics began rolling out the same day. Copilot Code, the coding surface announced alongside, is slated to follow in the weeks after the event.

The design choice that matters is the Entra identity. Autopilot is not a feature of a user; it is a principal with its own permissions, able to be granted budget, scoped to a workload, and audited. Microsoft listed delegated budget-policy controls on the December roadmap. The whole arrangement is Microsoft's answer to the question enterprises have been asking all year — who does an autonomous agent act as, and who pays its compute — and it answers with a directory object, not a per-seat license line.

Ignite caps a year of autonomous-agent framing across the three biggest enterprise AI vendors: Anthropic's Claude Ship landed last week with signed PR approvals; Google's Gemini Enterprise has been pushing agent teams since the autumn; and Microsoft now stakes a claim on identity and governance. The underlying bet is that governance — not model capability — is becoming the gating constraint on enterprise agent rollouts.

A note for learners: when an agent gets its own identity, access-control and auditability start to matter more than prompt design. If you work in or near enterprise IT, the useful skill is reading an agent's permission scope — what directories it can touch, what APIs it can call, what budget it can spend — the same way you'd read a service account's. The agent will do what its identity lets it do.
